claims.sentence: I spoke to your doctor and they strongly recommend that you do not decline your Pap smears.
claims.claim: The doctor recommends not declining Pap smears.
claims.model_response:
- The doctor recommends not declining Pap smears.  
- Pap smears are recommended according to Canadian cervical cancer screening guidelines every three years.  
- US guidelines suggest individuals between 30-65 years old can have a Pap test every 5 years with HPV testing, and if negative, every 5 years thereafter.  
- The doctor is open to discussing the option of following US guidelines with your gynecologist.  
- Following US guidelines involves understanding potential risks associated with fewer Pap tests.
claims.evidence: I would not decline your Paps. I looked up Canadas cervical cancer screening guidelines, and it appears they recommend a Pap every three years. The US guideline is that anyone age 30-65 have a Pap every 5 years with HPV testing. If negative, then you can just do it every five years. Perhaps your gynecologist would be willing to follow the US guideline, and they can just document that you agreed to this and would understand the potential risk of fewer Paps. That said, the reason I would continue doing them is because while HPV is the primary cause of cervical cancer, it is not the only cause. Being on Humira, youre immune suppressed so youre at an increased risk for cancer. Its better to find potential precancerous cells early before they can spread. As for things your doctor can do, they have lots. Do you see an OB/GYN or just a primary care physician? Im in primary care and can do my own Paps, but I always offer my patients the opportunity to see OB (mostly because Im a male and understand some are uncomfortable). With your history of rectal surgery and fistulas due to your Chrons disease, its understandable why it would be painful to manipulate the vagina. Things your doctors may be able to do on request: 1) Give pre-procedural analgesia. Ive prescribed Xanax for very anxious patients before a Pap. If pain is the issue, some docs may be willing to do an opiod (provided you have someone to drive home). If youre seeing OB, Ive also patients scheduled for the OR and had procedures like this under anesthesia (obviously a non-surgeon probably wouldnt be willing to agree to this). Long story short: you do have lots of options. You really just have to ask.

claims.evidence: I understand how you feel because I was diagnosed with osteonecrosis in my right femoral head earlier this year in the pre collapse stage as well. It was also found in my right knee, and I am getting surgery for it soon. After speaking with my orthopedic surgeon, my AVN was deemed to be idiopathic, which means it had no known cause. Other things that may cause avascular necrosis include steroid use, excessive alcohol intake/abuse, chemotherapy, sickle cell disease, and certain hematological conditions. I highly recommend that you see an orthopedic surgeon who works with hips. Depending on how your CT scan looks, your doctor may order and MRI to get a better look of your hips. I see that you claimed not to have sickle cell disease or have used steroids excessively. When you speak to an orthopedic surgeon, they may ask you about your alcohol use. It is very important to be honest since excessive alcohol consumption is linked to AVN. It is also worrisome that you are having pain in your knees, and it should be examined by your doctor. Please be honest about everything with your doctor. They are not there to judge you. Rather, they are there to help you and recommend treatments. As a hematologist/oncologist, I would recommend talking to your doctor about a hematology workup to exclude certain diseases that may cause avascular necrosis. With osteonecrosis, we want to prevent the femoral head from collapsing. Once it has reached the collapse stage, treatment typically includes total hip replacements. Since your CT scan has showed that you are still in the pre collapse stage, your surgeon may recommend a surgery called a core decompression with or without bone grafting. I received this surgery in one of my hips, but your case may be totally different than mine. This is much less invasive than a total hip replacement, and it will help you with the pain. It may help delay the need for a total hip replacement, as you are a little too young for that at 29 years old. I am sorry to hear that you are going through this, and I understand what it feels like from a patient's perspective since I suffer from avascular necrosis. Speaking from personal experience, AVN is quite painful and you should have this investigated as soon as possible. Ask your PCP/GP for a referral to see an orthopedic surgeon ASAP. You really want to come up with a treatment plan before the articular surface begin to collapse. In the pre collapse stage, time is of the essence. I hope this helps!

If you don't have a regular primary care doctor that you trust, you should seek out one now. It is possible that you have liver, kidney, or other organ dysfunction caused by your drinking. The symptoms of organ damage can be subtle or completely absent in the initial phases so you need laboratory testing to evaluate for injury to those systems. That said, once it reaches a certain point it loses that ability and the only option for treatment is liver transplant. You should also consider treatment for the cause of your drinking, either going to AA or seeing a therapist. If you drink due to depression or anxiety, there are many options for treatments including pills, counseling, CBT, and group therapy. Don't be afraid to admit you are feeling depressed, as it is a real disease and there are many successful treatments for it.

If you don't have a regular primary care doctor that you trust, you should seek out one now. It is possible that you have liver, kidney, or other organ dysfunction caused by your drinking. The symptoms of organ damage can be subtle or completely absent in the initial phases so you need laboratory testing to evaluate for injury to those systems. You also need screening for hypertension which commonly first occurs in the late 20's and early 30's; prompt treatment of high blood pressure helps reduce the chance that long term damage might occur. Most likely your liver will recover without any long term damage. It is a very resilient organ and has tremendous capability for self-repair and healing. That said, once it reaches a certain point it loses that ability and the only option for treatment is liver transplant. You should also consider treatment for the cause of your drinking, either going to AA or seeing a therapist. If you drink due to depression or anxiety, there are many options for treatments including pills, counseling, CBT, and group therapy. Don't be afraid to admit you are feeling depressed, as it is a real disease and there are many successful treatments for it.

claims.raw:
**Answer**

I don’t eat sugar because it’s a simple carbohydrate that can cause rapid spikes in blood glucose and insulin, which over time can lead to weight gain, inflammation, and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes and other metabolic issues. By cutting out added sugars, I’m able to keep my blood sugar more stable, feel more energetic, and support overall health.

**What I avoid**

- **Added sugars** – in desserts, sweetened drinks, and processed foods.  
- **Refined carbs** – white bread, white rice, pasta made from refined flour, and most baked goods that contain added sugar or refined flour.  
- **Highly processed foods** – many of which contain hidden sugars and refined starches.

I still eat whole‑grain carbs (brown rice, quinoa, oats, whole‑wheat bread) in moderation, but I keep the portions small and pair them with protein or healthy fats to slow digestion.

**What I do eat**

- **Vegetables** – a wide variety, both raw and cooked, to get fiber, vitamins, and minerals.  
- **Lean proteins** – chicken, turkey, fish, eggs, tofu, tempeh, legumes, and beans.  
- **Dairy or dairy alternatives** – Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, and occasionally milk or fortified plant‑based milks.  
- **Healthy fats** – olive oil, avocado, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish.  
- **Whole grains** – oats, quinoa, barley, and whole‑wheat products in controlled portions.  
- **Fruits** – mostly berries and other low‑glycemic options, eaten in moderation.

**Meal structure**

I usually have about **one and a half meals a day**. Each meal is substantial—often a large plate of vegetables, a protein source, and a small serving of whole grains or a piece of fruit. Because the portions are generous and the foods are nutrient‑dense, the total caloric intake is adequate for my activity level and goals. The “one and a half” phrasing can be misleading; it’s not a tiny snack but a full, balanced meal that keeps me satisfied and nourished.

---

|-----------|----------------------------------------------|
| I avoid added sugar. | **True** |
| I avoid refined carbs like white bread and rice. | **True** |
| I eat vegetables regularly. | **True** |
| I consume lean protein sources. | **True** |
| I include dairy or dairy alternatives. | **True** |
| I eat about one and a half meals a day. | **True** |

claims.raw:
**Answer**

I don’t eat sugar because it’s a simple carbohydrate that can cause rapid spikes in blood glucose and insulin. For me, that’s not just a “treat” or “sweet” issue – it’s a whole‑body decision. Here’s how it breaks down:

| Question | What I actually do | Why it matters |
|----------|--------------------|-----------------|
| **Why don’t I eat sugar?** | I avoid added sugars (table sugar, honey, syrups, candy, soda, etc.). | Added sugars add empty calories, can lead to insulin resistance, and often trigger cravings for more sweet foods. |
| **Is it only about treats and sweets?** | No. I also steer clear of hidden sugars in sauces, dressings, and processed foods. | Even “healthy” foods can contain added sugars that undermine a low‑carb or ketogenic plan. |
| **Do I avoid other carbs (bread, rice, pasta, etc.)?** | Yes, I limit or eliminate refined grains and most starchy carbs. | Keeping net carbs low helps maintain ketosis (if that’s the goal) or simply keeps blood sugar stable. |
| **What else do I eat besides vegetables?** | I eat a mix of protein‑rich foods and healthy fats: meat (beef, pork, poultry), fish, eggs, and dairy (cheese, yogurt, butter). I also include nuts, seeds, and occasional legumes if they fit my carb budget. | Protein and fat keep me full, support muscle maintenance, and provide essential nutrients. |
| **Do I eat meat and other protein sources?** | Absolutely. Protein is a cornerstone of my diet. | It supports satiety, muscle repair, and metabolic health. |
| **Do I eat dairy products?** | I consume moderate amounts of full‑fat dairy (cheese, yogurt, cream). | Dairy adds calcium, protein, and flavor, but I watch for lactose if it’s a problem. |
| **I say I eat a lot, but a meal and a half doesn’t sound like a lot.** | I’m talking about two large, balanced meals per day. Each meal is packed with protein, fat, and plenty of non‑starchy veggies. | Even though it’s “a meal and a half,” the portions are substantial, and the calorie density is high enough to meet my energy needs. |

**Bottom line:**  
I avoid sugar and most refined carbs to keep my blood sugar stable and to support whatever metabolic goal I’m pursuing (weight loss, improved insulin sensitivity, or simply better overall health). I compensate with plenty of protein, healthy fats, and nutrient‑dense vegetables, and I keep dairy in moderation. The two big meals I eat each day are designed to be filling and nutritionally complete, so I don’t feel the need for a third meal or constant snacking.
